work_order.understanding: The previous attempt's DIAGNOSIS was right and I am not rewriting it. I reproduced all four of its claims against 9f65cfd: expectedContribution did return 0 for an unrepresentable record, the seed did exit 0 with 'already present, nothing new written' over a planted stale row, money() did bake in a rupee sign, and the evaluate false-branch was only reachable from a unit test. Its five fixes landed and QA passed AC-1, AC-3, AC-4, AC-5, AC-7, AC-8 outright — 13 of 16 QA tests green, every page/state combination 200, no NaN, no 5xx in any HAR. What was wrong was the APPROACH, in one specific way: the plan diagnosed 'this build cannot read this record' as a property and then implemented it by hand at each of the four sites, each time against the two money keys its own diagnosis happened to be about. So 'a record this build cannot read' exists four times in this PR with four different definitions — src/data/repositories.js:595-601 checks 0 of 8 components and only for null/undefined, src/domain/opportunities.js:165 checks 3 of 8 with Number.isSafeInteger, scripts/seed.js:320 checks 2 of 8 with Number.isSafeInteger, src/web/pages.js:198 checks the 2 money keys at render time. The plan's own acceptance criterion was written at the level of the concept (AC-2: every opportunity row carries all EIGHT component keys) and the fix was written at the level of the keys, so the criterion and the code were never going to meet. That is the whole of BUG-1, BUG-2 and BUG-3, and it is why one ticket produced three findings on the same underlying defect. Reproduced myself against the PR branch, all three, none of them needing a planted record to be exotic: a stored record with pSuccess deleted returns 7 keys with expected_contribution_micros null; a record with value_micros 5000000.5 returns 8 keys with the float intact AND expected_contribution_micros null in the same body; a record with value_micros '2000000000' returns the string intact AND null; and a seed record with only pSuccess deleted re-seeds to a clean exit-0 no-op. I then prototyped the fix named below and confirmed it closes all three, keeps the pre-rename throw (test/ops/seed.test.js:70's case still throws, naming value_micros and cost_micros), and leaves 241 of 242 tests green — the single failure is that test's own /micros rename/ message assertion, which the work order below generalises rather than drops. One consequence the plan missed and this change picks up: money() today renders a negative micros as '-1.00', so AC-7's own claim that malformed money degrades to the em-dash was quietly false for negatives; routing the renderer through the shared rule makes it true. Explicitly NOT changing any acceptance criterion: AC-2 says what it should say, the code was wrong, and this is not the case where rewriting the criterion is correct. None of the three bugs is introduced_by_pr — the base commit has the same four undefined predicates — but all three contradict criteria this PR owns and this PR is what turns the surface into a stated contract, so they are fixed here.
work_order.root_cause: The app learned to validate opportunity components on the way IN (validateOpportunity, src/domain/opportunities.js:54-115, which already owns the exact rule: money is a non-negative safe integer of micros, every other component is a finite number) and was then taught by this PR to degrade honestly on the way OUT — but nowhere on the read side is that existing rule consulted. Every consumer of a STORED record re-derives 'can I stand behind this number' from scratch, against whichever keys the bug that motivated it happened to involve, so the four consumers disagree: the wire projection checks 0 of 8 components and only for null/undefined (so an absent non-money key is dropped by JSON.stringify, and a float or numeric string money passes through untouched); the contribution checks 3 of 8; the seed guard checks 2 of 8; the renderer checks 2. Because 'readable' is defined locally and never derived from the domain's COMPONENTS list, no consumer can be right about a record another one calls unreadable, and the PR's own present-and-null wire contract is narrower than the criterion that states it. The defect is the duplication, not any one of the four sites: fixing a fifth site by hand is what produced this failure.
work_order.approach:
One exported definition in the domain, derived from COMPONENTS, consumed by all four sites. This replaces the four hand-rolled predicates rather than adding a fifth, and it is a genuinely different approach from attempt 1 — attempt 1 hand-patched each site against the two money keys its own diagnosis was about; this derives the rule from the component list the domain already has and lets every site agree by construction.

(1) src/domain/opportunities.js gains the shared rule, next to the existing isFiniteNumber helper and built on the private COMPONENTS/MONEY_COMPONENTS constants. Three exports: unreadableComponents(record) returns the array of component keys this build cannot stand behind; isReadableOpportunityRecord(record) is that array's length === 0; readableComponents(record) is the wire projection, all eight keys present, each value passed through when readable and null when not. All three sit on one non-exported isReadableComponent(key, value): MONEY_COMPONENTS must be a non-negative safe integer, every other component must be a finite number (Number.isFinite, which does not coerce, so the string '2000000000' is unreadable). Keep COMPONENTS private — readableComponents builds the projection from it internally, so no new export of the list itself is needed. Document what the rule answers and what it does not: 'is this number trustworthy', not 'does the record satisfy every domain range'. A stored pSuccess of 1.5 is out of range but is still a number the build can print, so it stays on the wire; re-running full validation on a read path would be a different and much larger change (see alternatives_considered).

(2) expectedContribution keeps its current behaviour and stops carrying its own copy of the rule: its three guards become isReadableComponent('value_micros', ...), ('cost_micros', ...) and ('pSuccess', ...). The guard still stands in front of the arithmetic — a null reaching `valueMicros * pSuccess` is 0, which would turn 'unknown' into a confident break-even — and the comment explaining why must survive the edit.

(3) src/data/repositories.js shape() replaces its eight hand-written component lines with `components: readableComponents(record)`. One call, and it is the projection that decides the wire format, so the place QA found the two `?? null` and the six raw passthroughs both disappears rather than being corrected in place. The existing comment block goes with it and is rewritten to say what the new contract actually is: eight keys always; an unreadable component is present-and-null, never a dropped key (JSON.stringify removes undefined) and never a number this build cannot stand behind. The wire-format-change note stays, and its example is corrected — it currently illustrates absent-versus-null with 'value_micros' in components, which is precisely the distinction the new rule erases for that key. `record` itself is deliberately left verbatim (see risks).

(4) src/web/pages.js money() drops its own Number.isSafeInteger check for isReadableComponent('value_micros', micros), importing it from the domain alongside the money.js pair. pages.js already imports from domain/measurement.js, domain/decisions.js and domain/money.js, so a fourth domain import is consistent with the file. This is what makes 'one renderer, one rule' true rather than aspirational, and it fixes a real gap attempt 1 left open: a negative micros is a safe integer, so today it renders '-1.00' and AC-7's claim that malformed money degrades to the em-dash is false for it. pages.js:663's `raw == null` guard is untouched and still covers the nulls the projection now produces; the two guards overlap harmlessly and the view must not call the domain (it is handed a projected row).

(5) scripts/seed.js deletes its local isReadableOpportunityRecord entirely and imports the domain's. Because the rule is no longer money-only, the OPP_STALE_RECORD message can no longer claim the record 'predates the micros rename' — that is a guess about the cause, and it is wrong for every shape except the one attempt 1 found. The message now names the component keys unreadableComponents returned and states the rule those keys failed ('money must be a non-negative integer number of micros; every other component must be a finite number'), then keeps the recovery, which is unchanged and still the only one that works. details carries {opportunity_id, unreadable_components} instead of the hardcoded field: 'value_micros'. The non-atomic comment above the check stays exactly as it is.

(6) test/ops/seed.test.js's assertion `assert.match(thrown.message, /micros rename/, 'and why this build cannot read it')` is GENERALISED, never dropped: it becomes an assertion that the message names the unreadable component keys (value_micros and cost_micros for the pre-rename fixture it plants). This is the fifth place the same over-narrow definition is written down, and leaving it would mean the next person to change the message deletes the assertion instead of fixing it. Every other assertion in that test — the code, the /^OPP_STALE_RECORD/ prefix, the id, the recovery, details.opportunity_id — stays as it is.

Not in this change, deliberately: `record` on the wire stays verbatim (risks), the domain range rules stay write-side only (alternatives_considered), and no existing criterion is edited (understanding).

files.change: Add the one shared definition, beside the existing isFiniteNumber helper and built on the private COMPONENTS and MONEY_COMPONENTS constants. A non-exported isReadableComponent(key, value): MONEY_COMPONENTS.includes(key) requires Number.isSafeInteger(value) && value >= 0, every other key requires isFiniteNumber(value) — which is typeof 'number' plus Number.isFinite, so a numeric string is unreadable rather than coerced. Three exports on top of it: unreadableComponents(record) returns COMPONENTS.filter over the rule (the array of keys, not a boolean — the seed message and details need to name them); isReadableOpportunityRecord(record) is unreadableComponents(record).length === 0; readableComponents(record) builds the eight-key projection, each value passed through when readable and null when not, in COMPONENTS order. Doc-comment all three with what the rule answers and what it deliberately does not: 'can this build stand behind this number', not 'does this record satisfy every domain range' — a stored pSuccess of 1.5 is out of range but is still a number the build can print. Keep COMPONENTS itself private; readableComponents derives the projection from it internally so the list does not become a fourth thing to keep in sync. Then rewrite expectedContribution's three inline guards (currently the Number.isSafeInteger/isFiniteNumber trio at what is now the middle of the function) to call isReadableComponent('value_micros', valueMicros), isReadableComponent('cost_micros', costMicros) and isReadableComponent('pSuccess', pSuccess). Its behaviour is unchanged — same three keys, same rule, same null — and the comment explaining why the guard stands IN FRONT of the arithmetic (a null reaching `valueMicros * pSuccess` is 0, which would turn 'unknown' into a confident break-even) must survive the edit verbatim in substance, because it is the only thing stopping a future reader from 'simplifying' the guard back behind the arithmetic. Extend the module header comment by one line naming the read-side rule as the twin of validateOpportunity's write-side rules.
files.why: This is the defect: the rule already exists on the write side in validateOpportunity (src/domain/opportunities.js:54-115 — money is a non-negative safe integer, other components are finite numbers) and four read-side consumers never consult it. Putting it here is the only place all four can reach — the module is pure (no IO, no sqlite, per its own header) and is already imported by src/data/repositories.js:11 and scripts/seed.js:10.

files.change: In createOpportunityRepository's shape(), replace the eight hand-written component lines with a single `components: readableComponents(record)`. files.why: This is the projection that decides the wire format and the site of BUG-1 and BUG-2. alternatives_considered.approach: Patch the three sites individually: add `?? null` to the other six components in shape(), swap the repositories' `?? null` for Number.isSafeInteger on the two money keys, and widen scripts/seed.js's guard to all eight with an inline COMPONENTS loop.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: This is the same approach as attempt 1 with the same failure mode — four definitions instead of three, still hand-written, still able to drift at the next edit, and it is what the QA hint would have described as a fifth patch rather than a fix. It fixes exactly the three fixtures QA happened to plant. The defect is the duplication; leaving four copies of a rule in place is the defect.

alternatives_considered.approach: Normalise the stored `record` blob as well as `components`, so a float money value never appears anywhere in the response body.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It makes the response stop describing what is actually stored, which is the one thing `record` is for — an operator debugging a corrupt row needs to see the corruption, not a laundered copy of it. It is also a second wire-format change nobody asked for. Recorded in risks instead, so the decision is visible rather than accidental.

alternatives_considered.approach: Make the read-side rule a full re-validation of the stored record — isReadableOpportunityRecord = validateOpportunity(record).ok — so out-of-range components such as a stored pSuccess of 1.5 also read null.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It conflates 'is this number trustworthy' with 'does this record satisfy every domain rule', and it silently widens the wire contract far past what the three bugs require: a stored pSuccess of 1.5 would vanish from the response on a read path that is otherwise a display path. validateOpportunity also wants opportunity_id/tenant_id/name and returns an error object, so using it as a predicate on the read path is heavier for no gain. The type-level rule is what the contribution, the renderer and the seed guard actually need. Pinned as a deliberate boundary by a test so a later agent cannot widen it by accident.

alternatives_considered.approach: Fix the three bugs and leave pages.js's local guard alone, treating the renderer as a fifth site that already behaves correctly.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: It is not correct: Number.isSafeInteger(-1000000) is true, so a negative micros renders '-1.00' today and AC-7's own claim that malformed money degrades to the em-dash is false for it. And leaving it local is what makes AC-12 untrue, which is the whole point of this attempt.

alternatives_considered.approach: Narrow AC-2 to the pre-rename shape only, as the QA report's coverage_gaps section offers ('if the maintainers consider a record missing a non-money component out of scope, BUG-1 and BUG-3 should be dropped').
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: That would be rewriting a criterion to match a defect, which is the artefact this pipeline must never produce. The criterion says every row carries all eight keys; the code normalised two of eight; the code is wrong. The PR's own stated premise is records written by a build other than this one, and a build other than this one may have written a record missing any component. AC-2 stands unchanged, and AC-9/AC-10/AC-11 are added alongside it to make the three specific shapes checkable on their own.

alternatives_considered.approach: Make the seed repair the stale row instead of throwing — rewrite the stored record at the fixed seed id, which would make the guard unnecessary.
alternatives_considered.rejected_because: The seed is INSERT OR IGNORE by fixed id and deliberately never rewrites a stored record; a repair path would silently overwrite data an operator may be debugging, and it contradicts the recovery the error currently gives. Out of scope and unchanged from attempt 1's reasoning.

Not environmental. The preview was up, all 16 QA tests ran, and CI is green. All three bugs reproduce deterministically on the PR branch with a two-line fixture each, and I fixed all three in a prototype that kept 241 of 242 tests green. Nothing here needs a person.

assumptions: The preview that QA tested is the same build the implementer will work against. I reproduced against origin/sdlc/issue-40 at 9f65cfd, not against a local preview, and my reproduction is at the repository and seed level (no browser needed) because all three bugs are in the data path.

A stored record with a non-money component missing or corrupt is in scope, because the PR's own premise — stated in the routes.js CONTRACT comment and in the seed guard — is that records may have been written by a build other than this one. AC-2 as written already asserts the eight-key guarantee for every row, so narrowing it would be moving a goalpost rather than scoping the work.

The money rule stays 'non-negative safe integer of micros', matching validateOpportunity's OPP_BAD_MONEY check, which is stricter than the three read-side sites that only tested Number.isSafeInteger. Adopting the write-side rule is what makes AC-7 true for negative money.

Only a non-negative, finite-number check belongs on the read path. Range validation (pSuccess in [0,1], infoValue >= 0, the numerator product) stays write-side; a stored record outside those ranges is still made of numbers the build can print, and nulling it would be a contract change nobody asked for.
unknowns: Whether any consumer outside this repository distinguishes `'value_micros' in components` from `components.value_micros === null`. The change makes that distinction disappear for all eight keys, because an unreadable component is now always present-and-null. Within this repo nothing reads `components` except the route and the view, and both treat the two the same — but the PR already flagged this as a wire-format change and this widens it from two keys to eight. Stated in AC-2's own text and in risks rather than resolved, because it is not resolvable from inside the repo.

Whether a non-INR tenant can be made to draw a page in a live browser. Unchanged from attempt 1 and still true: firstTenant() renders tenants.list()[0], which is ORDER BY created_at, id (src/data/repositories.js:27), so a USD tenant created after the demo one is never the tenant a page draws. AC-5 stays test-verified. This change does not touch currency threading, so nothing here makes it worse — but it also does not make it better, and QA should be told so rather than discovering it as a coverage gap again.

Whether the OPP_STALE_RECORD message wording change breaks anything that greps for 'micros rename'. Nothing in this repo does; the one assertion that did is being generalised rather than removed. An operator's runbook outside the repo might, and the message is the only guidance they get, so the change is worth a line in the PR body.
risks: `record` on the wire is left verbatim while `components` is projected, so a corrupt row still shows its raw float or string under `record` even though `components` now says null. This is deliberate — `record` is the stored blob and exists to be debugged — but it is the one place a client can still see the number we refuse to stand behind. If QA files it, the answer is that it is a recorded decision, not an oversight, and changing it means deciding what `record` is for.

Broadening the seed guard to all eight components makes it fire on strictly more databases. A healthy current-shape seed is unaffected (I re-ran it: same counters, clean no-op, exit 0), but a database written by a build that stored an out-of-format non-money component will now exit non-zero where attempt 1 exited 0. That is the intent — a clean no-op over an unreadable row is what the guard exists to prevent — and AC-8's note about CI scripts already covers the exit-code change from attempt 1.

The OPP_STALE_RECORD message no longer asserts a cause. A record missing pSuccess now produces a message that names the component rather than saying it predates the micros rename, which is a weaker story for the common case and a correct one for the rest. The recovery line is unchanged and is the part an operator acts on.

pages.js gains a fourth domain import (src/domain/opportunities.js) purely for the money guard. The file already imports three domain modules, so this is consistent, but it does make the view depend on the opportunity domain for rendering a number — the alternative, passing a predicate in, was rejected as more coupling, not less.

The cross-consumer agreement table in test/domain/opportunity-readability.test.js is the only thing standing between this fix and a fifth hand-rolled definition, and it is a unit test: it proves the four consumers agree, not that a future contributor imports the domain version. The review grep in AC-12 is the human half of that and cannot be automated into the test suite here.

`.sdlc/memory/patterns/` is still empty and the pattern this ticket exposes — 'a rule re-derived at each consumer instead of derived once from the domain's component list' — is exactly the entry a future agent would want after this merges. I cannot write it: .sdlc/memory/** is off limits to any ticket. Flagging it here for the Librarian.
out_of_scope: Rewriting or deleting any existing acceptance criterion. AC-1 through AC-8 stand verbatim, in place, with the same ids and numbers; AC-9 through AC-12 are additions.

The domain range rules (pSuccess in [0,1], infoValue non-negative, the numerator product) on the read path — see alternatives_considered for why re-validating on read is a different and larger change.
Normalising the `record` blob on the wire — see risks.

Currency threading, ISO_CURRENCIES coverage and the formatMoney minor-unit question. Attempt 1 fixed what it fixed and QA passed AC-4 and AC-5; this change touches pages.js only for the readability guard.

The evaluate deduplication path, the seed's non-atomic boundary, and the eight-key-versus-range tension in validateOpportunity — all recorded by QA as coverage gaps rather than bugs, and none of them is what failed.
Writing .sdlc/memory/patterns/. The Librarian's, and off limits to a ticket.
residual_risks: My prototype replaced the eight component lines in shape() with one call, which is the cleanest shape for the fix, but it is a judgement call: an implementer could instead keep the eight lines and wrap each value in isReadableComponent. Both are correct; the single call is what makes it impossible for a key to be left out, which is the entire failure being fixed. If the eight-line form is used, say so in the PR body — it is exactly the shape that produced BUG-1.

My prototype's OPP_STALE_RECORD wording is a starting point, not a specification. The constraint is that it names the unreadable component keys, does not assert a cause it cannot know, and keeps the recovery. The exact phrasing is the implementer's call.

I verified the prototype with node --test (241 of 242, the one failure being the message-text assertion this work order tells the implementer to generalise) and by direct reproduction of all three bugs plus the pre-rename regression. I did not run it against a live preview in a browser — the view change is one guard behind an existing em-dash return, and the qa_script's browser sweep is what confirms it end to end.

The new domain exports widen a module's public surface. Nothing in the repo treats src/domain/opportunities.js as a stable public API, and three call sites already import from it, so the risk is naming rather than structure.
work_order.confidence_rationale: High because this is not a diagnosis from a symptom: I extracted the PR branch at 9f65cfd, reproduced all three bugs myself with two-line fixtures (7 keys for a record missing pSuccess; a float and a string money value sitting beside a null contribution on the same wire body; a clean exit-0 seed no-op over a record whose only damage is a deleted pSuccess), then prototyped the fix and confirmed it closes all three while keeping the pre-rename throw and 241 of 242 tests green. The one failing test is the message-text assertion this work order explicitly generalises rather than drops. I also found a fourth instance the QA report did not file — pages.js renders a negative micros as '-1.00', so AC-7's own claim was quietly false for negatives — and confirmed that on the real formatter rather than asserting it. What keeps it off the low 90s: the wording of the seed error message is a judgement call the implementer owns, `record` deliberately stays raw and a future QA run may reasonably file it, and I verified the fix at the repository and seed level rather than in a live browser.

review.title: The CONTRACT comment added to POST /v1/opportunities states a wire contract that is false. It asserts `expected_contribution_micros` 'is null exactly when one or more of the components in this same body is null' and that 'a client that null-checks one can rely on the other agreeing'. expectedContribution consults only value_micros, cost_micros and pSuccess (src/domain/opportunities.js:232-234), so a body can carry a null component next to a confident numeric contribution. A client written against this comment is wrong for every stored record whose only damage is one of the other five components.
review.detail:
The CONTRACT comment added to POST /v1/opportunities states a wire contract that is false. It asserts `expected_contribution_micros` 'is null exactly when one or more of the components in this same body is null' and that 'a client that null-checks one can rely on the other agreeing'. expectedContribution consults only value_micros, cost_micros and pSuccess (src/domain/opportunities.js:232-234), so a body can carry a null component next to a confident numeric contribution. A client written against this comment is wrong for every stored record whose only damage is one of the other five components.

`src/api/routes.js:370`

Evidence: Stored record with valid micros money and pSuccess but fit stored as the numeric string '0.9'. Driven over HTTP through the PR's own repository projection:

  GET /v1/opportunities body.components = {"value_micros":6000000000,"pSuccess":0.6,"fit":null,"infoValue":1.2,"reversibility":0.9,"cost_micros":1900000000,"downside":2,"delay":1}
  POST /v1/opportunities (idempotent re-post) components.fit = null  expected_contribution_micros = 1700000000

Same result for each of the five components the arithmetic never reads: `node -e` over isReadableComponent/readableComponents/expectedContribution with infoValue, reversibility, downside and delay each set to '0.9' gives `unreadable=["<key>"]`, `components null at ["<key>"]`, `expected_contribution_micros=1700000000` in all five cases.

The PR contradicts itself: test/domain/opportunity-readability.test.js:96-97 states the correct rule in a comment — 'The contribution reads value_micros, cost_micros and pSuccess' — while routes.js:370-373 generalises it to all eight. AC-10 itself is met for money components; the defect is the client-facing restatement of it, which reaches past money to fit, infoValue, reversibility, downside and delay.

Fix: Narrow the claim to the components the contribution actually reads. Something like: 'expected_contribution_micros is computed from value_micros, cost_micros and pSuccess alone, so it is null exactly when one of THOSE THREE is null. A null in any of the other five components does not affect it — a corrupt fit still yields a confident number here. Money is the case that matters, and for money the two halves do agree: a component the build cannot stand behind is null in components, and the contribution is null in the same body.'

review.title: The CONTRACT comment's biconditional is false in the direction Reviewer A did not check. It claims expected_contribution_micros 'is null exactly when one or more of the components in this same body is null'. A found a null component beside a confident number. The converse also holds: a body where ALL EIGHT components are readable and non-null, and the contribution is null. Reviewer A's proposed fix — narrow the claim to the three keys the contribution reads — does not fix this, because no narrowing of the key set can: the null here comes from the arithmetic overflow guard, not from a component.
review.detail:
The CONTRACT comment's biconditional is false in the direction Reviewer A did not check. It claims expected_contribution_micros 'is null exactly when one or more of the components in this same body is null'. A found a null component beside a confident number. The converse also holds: a body where ALL EIGHT components are readable and non-null, and the contribution is null. Reviewer A's proposed fix — narrow the claim to the three keys the contribution reads — does not fix this, because no narrowing of the key set can: the null here comes from the arithmetic overflow guard, not from a component.

`src/api/routes.js:370`

Evidence: Driven over HTTP against the PR branch, storing value_micros 9007199254740991 (MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, a legal non-negative safe integer) with pSuccess 1.5 (a finite number, so readable under the rule, merely out of range) and everything else healthy:

  GET  /v1/opportunities  opp_qa_ovf_010 components = {"value_micros":9007199254740991,"pSuccess":1.5,"fit":0.9,"infoValue":1.2,"reversibility":0.9,"cost_micros":1900000000,"downside":2,"delay":1}
  POST /v1/opportunities  expected_contribution_micros = null,  nulls in components = []

Both components are readable, so readableComponents passes them through; the guard at src/domain/opportunities.js:230-234 passes; then valueMicros * pSuccess overflows MAX_SAFE_INTEGER, Math.trunc leaves it inexact, and :240 returns null. Reachable under this PR's own premise — the record was written by a build that did not range-check pSuccess, which is exactly the record class AC-9 through AC-11 exist for. The same shape falls out of pSuccess = 1e300, which I also confirmed.

So a client that null-checks the components and concludes 'the contribution is a number' is wrong here, just as a client that null-checks the contribution and concludes 'some component is null' is wrong in A's case. Both halves of 'exactly when' fail, in opposite directions.

Fix: Drop the biconditional and state only the direction that is actually true, which is the one AC-10 is about: expected_contribution_micros is null whenever value_micros, cost_micros or pSuccess is unreadable, and components reports each of those as null in the same body — so a null contribution always comes with a null money component, and a client may rely on that direction. Say explicitly that the reverse does not hold: a null in any of the other five components leaves the contribution a number, and an all-readable body can still carry a null contribution when the arithmetic overflows. Then say the money case is the one that matters and it does agree.

review.title: money() reaches into the opportunity domain to ask a question that has nothing to do with opportunities. It calls isReadableComponent('value_micros', micros) — a function named for a component key, from the opportunity module — to validate a Meta ad-set budget, a Meta insight spend, an experiment cap and a Qualified CPL. None of those is an opportunity component. The view now depends on the opportunity domain for rendering a number that came from the Meta integration or the experiments domain.

money() reaches into the opportunity domain to ask a question that has nothing to do with opportunities. It calls isReadableComponent('value_micros', micros) — a function named for a component key, from the opportunity module — to validate a Meta ad-set budget, a Meta insight spend, an experiment cap and a Qualified CPL. None of those is an opportunity component. The view now depends on the opportunity domain for rendering a number that came from the Meta integration or the experiments domain.

`src/web/pages.js:213`

Evidence: Call sites of money(): src/web/pages.js:191 (META_CELLS.adSets, daily_budget_micros from the Meta provider), :193 (META_CELLS.insights, spend_micros), :384 (kpiStrip, qualified_cpl_micros from domain/measurement.js:217), :770 and :772 (experimentCard, caps.max_spend_micros and caps.max_downside_micros from domain/experiments.js). The value passed is never an opportunity component, and the key 'value_micros' is a fiction supplied to satisfy a component-keyed signature.

The check itself is not a reinvention — domain/money.js:40 already owns 'is this a valid integer number of micros' in assertValidMicros. That one throws; this one returns a boolean, which is the actual difference, and a boolean sibling there would be a two-line addition rather than a cross-domain import. The work order's alternatives_considered considered passing a predicate in and rejected it as more coupling; it does not appear to have considered putting the money half of the rule in money.js, which is strictly less coupling.

The concrete cost is that the rule now has a second, unintended blast radius: tighten the opportunity money rule and Meta spend rendering silently changes with it, with nothing in either file to say so.

Fix: Export the money half of the rule under its own name and let money.js own it — isReadableMoney(micros) in src/domain/money.js, with isReadableComponent delegating to it for MONEY_COMPONENTS — and have pages.js import that instead. One definition of 'a number of micros this build can stand behind', in the module that already owns micros, and no fourth domain import in the view. If the cross-domain import is kept deliberately, say why in the work order so the next reader does not read it as an accident.

review.detail:
AC-12 claims 'a component this build can stand behind' has exactly one definition derived from the domain's COMPONENTS list, and the review grep it specifies does not catch the one hand-picked key subset that is still outside the domain. src/web/pages.js declares its own MONEY_COMPONENTS = new Set(['value_micros', 'cost_micros']) — a second, hand-maintained copy of the domain's money-key list — and uses it at :694 to decide which components render through money(). This is the exact shape AC-12 says must not exist, one file over from the change.

`src/web/pages.js:685`

Evidence: src/web/pages.js:685 and src/domain/opportunities.js:32 both list value_micros and cost_micros by hand. The view's list is pre-existing (origin/main:663) and the work order explicitly declines to touch that line ('Leave the view's consumer at src/web/pages.js:663 exactly as it is'), so this is not introduced by the PR — but it is the one place where the PR's central invariant is not true, and a reviewer grepping for Number.isSafeInteger per AC-12 will not surface it. It is not a readability check, so AC-12's letter is satisfied while its intent is not; that gap is the finding.

The drift is not hypothetical: the set decides formatting, so a component added to the domain's money list and not to the view's would render as a bare number while every other consumer treated it as money.

Fix: Either export the money-key set from the domain and import it here, or state in AC-12 and the PR body that the guarantee covers the readability rule only, not the view's formatting list, so the next agent does not read AC-12 as covering both.

review.title: isReadableOpportunityRecord is an exported one-line wrapper with exactly one production caller, and that caller re-derives the array on the next line to build its message — so the export buys a second traversal of the same record and a fifth name for one rule. unreadableComponents already answers the question; the boolean is unreadableComponents(record).length === 0, and the seed guard has to call unreadableComponents anyway.
review.detail:
isReadableOpportunityRecord is an exported one-line wrapper with exactly one production caller, and that caller re-derives the array on the next line to build its message — so the export buys a second traversal of the same record and a fifth name for one rule. unreadableComponents already answers the question; the boolean is unreadableComponents(record).length === 0, and the seed guard has to call unreadableComponents anyway.

`src/domain/opportunities.js:92`

Evidence: The only production caller is scripts/seed.js:332, `if (previous && !isReadableOpportunityRecord(previous.record))`, and eight lines later at :340, `const unreadable = unreadableComponents(previous.record)`. Two traversals of an eight-key array to decide a branch and then name its contents. isReadableOpportunityRecord appears nowhere else in src/ or scripts/ outside these two lines and the test file.

The work order asked for all three exports and justified the array over the boolean on the grounds that the message needs the keys. That reasoning is sound and the boolean is defensible for readability at the guard — but as written the guard pays for the convenience twice, and the module's public surface grows by one name for it.

Fix: In scripts/seed.js, compute the array once and branch on its length — const unreadable = previous ? unreadableComponents(previous.record) : []; if (unreadable.length) { ... } — and drop the isReadableOpportunityRecord export. If the named boolean is worth keeping for the guard's readability, keep it and have the message interpolate from a single unreadableComponents call made before the branch, so only one traversal happens either way.

review.title: The diff a reviewer sees is roughly twice the change the work order describes, and the extra half is not identified anywhere in the PR. The branch carries two commits — f3043db, a superseded attempt, and a13c51f, the attempt this work order specifies — and about 605 of the 1170 insertions against main come from the superseded one. The work order describes those changes as pre-existing and lists them under out_of_scope, which is true of the branch and false of the PR: a reviewer approving PR #43 approves all of it, and the work order's own words for these lines contradict what the diff shows.
review.detail:
The diff a reviewer sees is roughly twice the change the work order describes, and the extra half is not identified anywhere in the PR. The branch carries two commits — f3043db, a superseded attempt, and a13c51f, the attempt this work order specifies — and about 605 of the 1170 insertions against main come from the superseded one. The work order describes those changes as pre-existing and lists them under out_of_scope, which is true of the branch and false of the PR: a reviewer approving PR #43 approves all of it, and the work order's own words for these lines contradict what the diff shows.

`src/domain/opportunities.js:240`

Evidence: git log origin/main..HEAD is f3043db then a13c51f. f3043db contributes 605 insertions across 9 files; a13c51f contributes 601 across 10. Two concrete mismatches a reviewer will hit:

1. src/web/pages.js: the currency threading (ISO_CURRENCIES import, the currency parameter through metaTable/metaRegions/opportunityRow/rankedList/experimentCard, the kpiStrip rewrite) is ~70 lines that the work order places out of scope and says must not be reworked. It is not in main — origin/main:src/web/pages.js has no ISO_CURRENCIES — so it is new in this diff.

2. src/domain/opportunities.js:240: the work order's files[] entry says expectedContribution's 'behaviour is unchanged — same three keys, same rule, same null'. Against main the PR changes `? contribution : 0` to `? contribution : null`, a wire-behaviour change (Reviewer A confirms the post-rename response carries null). That change is in f3043db. The work order's wording would lead a reviewer to believe the diff contains no behaviour change on this line.

The PR body lists per-file insertion counts and checks AC-4 and AC-5 — the criteria the work order calls out-of-scope — but never says the diff contains a superseded attempt, so nothing in the PR tells a reviewer which half they are being asked to approve now.

Fix: Say so in the PR body: one line naming that the branch carries a superseded attempt and that the reviewable change is a13c51f, with the f3043db lines called out as already-landed-in-this-branch. If the pipeline intends one PR per issue, note that attempt 1 was never split out, so the reviewer of #43 is reviewing both. Nothing needs to change in the code; this is about the reviewer being able to tell what they are approving.
